commit.message: kernel: susfs (LKM): sus_path: release inode holds at filesystem shutdown
kernel: susfs (LKM): susfs_fp: accept PAC call landing pads
kernel: susfs (LKM): opath: file_close_fd returns the file, not a status - one pointer per name
kernel: susfs (LKM): sus_path: tolerate missing BTF lifetime support
kernel: susfs (LKM): docs: clarify O_PATH close helper ABI

kernel: susfs (LKM): patch_memory: resolve the cache-flush helper by name at run time

The dcache/icache helper was picked at build time from the tree's cacheflush.h, so a module built
with 5.14+ headers carried an undefined dcache_clean_inval_poc - and a kernel that keeps the older
name refuses the load with "Unknown symbol dcache_clean_inval_poc (err -2)" (measured on a Samsung
5.x kernel, issue #77).  Which spelling a kernel carries is not decided by its version number.

- Both spellings are resolved by name at run time, the 5.14+ one first.
- A kernel carrying neither loses text/data patching instead of patching without the flush the
  write needs: ksu_patch_text_nosync() refuses before the store, and the two wrappers are
  __nocfi noinline like every other indirect kernel call in the module.
- kernel/Makefile no longer probes the headers, and the CI name list gains __flush_icache_range.

kernel: susfs (LKM): open_redirect: redirect at the name layer, hold nothing

The forward direction ran on a `vfs_open` kprobe, which needs the target's `struct path` cached in
the rule: a pinned dentry and mount is what kept a filesystem busy, so `umount` returned EBUSY for as
long as a rule existed.

The redirect now happens one layer up, at the NAME, in the syscall entry:

- kernel/susfs_or_entry.c (new) resolves the caller's path with getname_flags() + filename_lookup(),
  matches the rule, opens the target with filp_open() and returns the fd it installed itself instead
  of running the original syscall.  It hangs off the wrappers susfs_opath.c already installs for the
  open entries, because one syscall entry can carry only one wrapper, and it stays off unless those
  wrappers are really in the native openat/openat2 slots.
- A rule holds numbers plus a kstatfs snapshot - no dentry, no mount, no inode - so it no longer
  matters to umount.  Since nothing is pinned, a match also compares i_generation: a filesystem may
  reuse an inode number after a delete, and the number alone would then redirect an unrelated file.
- d_path and vfs_statfs answer the reverse disguise from that snapshot through return probes, reading
  their arguments in the entry probe (at return time only the return value is still in a register).
- What the skipped syscall would have done is reproduced where it is visible - the arm64 O_LARGEFILE
  bit, and IN_OPEN on the kernels that happen to carry an out-of-line fsnotify_open() (it is a static
  inline elsewhere, and the log says so there) - while anything this layer would answer differently
  from the kernel goes back to the kernel instead: a flag bit it would reject, a flags value whose
  upper half it ignores, and openat2's resolve/usize/mode, which it validates field by field.
- Deleting a rule marks it dead and leaves its fields in place: a name cleared under the reader that
  already matched it made filp_open("") resolve to the caller's own working directory.
- A redirected fd goes through the same O_PATH post-check as any other, so an O_PATH fd naming a
  sus_path-hidden file is still taken away.
- or_entry is on by default; or_entry=0, a missing symbol, or an O_PATH layer without those entries
  leaves the layer unarmed, and a rule is then refused instead of accepted and inert.
  susfs_open_redirect_rules counts live rules, so the extra lookup stops when the last rule is
  deleted.

Verified: CI green on all eight module variants plus tools and the two artifact gates (the run is linked in the PR), including the CFI call-site gate and the artifact
symbol checks.  On device (5.15.180, android13-5.15 artifact) a rule `tmpfs/target -> .../redirected`:
umount of that tmpfs with the rule still present returns 0 (EBUSY before), clear then umount also 0,
rmmod clean without WARN; the redirect still works for absolute, relative, symlink and dirfd-relative
opens with matching content and md5, and an unrelated open or an O_CREAT is untouched.  The reverse
faces register on every variant; they answer only for app processes, which that device cannot
produce, so they have no hardware evidence yet.

kernel: susfs (LKM): open_redirect: hand a rule's slot back instead of spending one per add

The rule table is a fixed array of slots and a slot was only ever appended to it, so the limit was
"how many rules were ever added" rather than "how many exist": 64 adds over the module's lifetime -
adds followed by deletes included - made every later add fail with -ENOSPC.  The scan bound grew the
same way.

- Deleting or replacing a rule now retires its slot; the slot is cleared and handed out again once a
  grace period has passed (or_reclaim_slot()).
- That is safe because every reader copies what it needs out of an entry while it holds
  rcu_read_lock: the name-layer hook copies the redirect target into a caller buffer (the interface
  no longer hands out a pointer into the table), the d_path face copies the name into its per-instance
  data in the entry probe, the statfs face copies the snapshot, and the maps and fdinfo faces read the
  entry inside one rcu section.  A slot may therefore only be reused after synchronize_rcu().
- Rewriting a rule takes the slot it releases, so a rewrite cannot fail with -ENOSPC; the capacity
  check stays ahead of any retirement, as before.
- /proc/susfs_open_redirect now decides "(empty)" by the live count, not by the scan bound.

Verified: CI green on all eight module variants plus tools, including the CFI call-site gate.

Support hot installing modules (https://github.com/tiann/KernelSU/pull/3901)

Official support for hot installing modules, so metamodules no longer
need to carry their own hack (e.g. https://github.com/backslashxx/mountify/commit/5bdfb8f). It
keeps the existing convention, so modules that already use it work
unchanged:

```sh
export MODULE_HOT_INSTALL_REQUEST=true
export MODULE_HOT_RUN_SCRIPT=hotinstall.sh   # optional
```

After the install script (including a metamodule's `metainstall.sh`)
succeeds, ksud:

1. Replaces `/data/adb/modules/<id>` with the staged dir. The old dir is
moved to `/data/adb/ksu/hot_install_trash/` and deleted on the next
post-fs-data, so processes and mounts still using it keep working until
then. If the move fails the old dir is restored and the regular path is
used.
2. Loads `sepolicy.rule` (rules are additive; dropped rules stay until
reboot).
3. Runs `MODULE_HOT_RUN_SCRIPT` from the live module dir via
`exec_script` (same env/cgroup/process group as boot scripts) in init's
mount namespace, waiting up to 30s.
4. Leaves no `update` flag.

It falls back to the regular reboot path, printing the reason, when
installing a metamodule, in safe mode, or when `MODULE_HOT_RUN_SCRIPT`
is not a relative path to a file in the module.

Only applied on the next boot: `system/` mounts, `system.prop`, `initrc`
and the boot stage scripts. The old version is not stopped and
`uninstall.sh` is not run; that is up to the hot run script.

- `installer.sh` exports `KSU_HAS_HOT_INSTALL=true`; metamodules can
skip their own implementation when it is set.
- Older metamodules that still swap the dirs themselves keep working:
the marker moves along with the module dir, ksud sees no request in
`modules_update` and takes the regular path (and removes the stray
marker).

The reboot button is only shown when a flashed module still has the
`update` flag.

`module.md` (new "Hot install" section, `KSU_HAS_HOT_INSTALL`) and
`metamodule.md`, en and zh_CN.

- `cargo clippy --target aarch64-linux-android --release` and
`:app:compileDebugKotlin` pass.
- Not yet tested on a device.

-com.rifsxd.ksunext: Port (Flash.kt / KsuCli.kt) and link showFloatAction (reboot FAB)

kernel: susfs (LKM): sus_mount: the mount prefix list holds 64 entries instead of 8

The list behind /proc/susfs_hide_mounts ("which mounts are ours") stopped at 8 prefixes, which a
container setup outgrows quickly.  It now holds 64.

Raising the constant alone does not build: SUS_MOUNT_KEEP_CMDLINE is derived from it and three
functions kept that buffer, or a list-sized array, on the stack - 8 KB frames, past the limit the
kernel allows (-Wframe-larger-than=2048).  So:

- sus_mount_keep_parse() scans the caller's string in place instead of copying it into that buffer
  first (nothing there rewrites it, and the callers already bound its length).
- sus_mount_keep_proc_write() takes its command buffer from kvmalloc().
- the init path stages the single default entry in a one-row array instead of one sized for the
  whole list.
- /proc/susfs_hide_mounts prints the list straight into the seq_file, and the sysfs parameter read
  says when it had to cut the text short (its buffer is capped at PAGE_SIZE, the node is not).

Verified: CI green on all eight module variants plus tools, including the CFI call-site gate.

kernel: susfs (LKM): sus_mount: read the prefix list from a snapshot, and keep the cut notice whole

Two things the 64-entry change left behind, both in the two read paths it rewrote.

The sysfs read reserved 96 bytes for the "N more; cat /proc/susfs_hide_mounts for
all" notice and then wrote the notice into that same room: with 64 prefixes of 127
characters the loop stopped 96 bytes from the end, the notice came out as
"... (33 more; cat /proc/susfs_hide_" and the final newline was lost with it - the
read that needs to say "there is more" was the one that could not. The reserve is
now one full prefix line plus the notice (SUS_MOUNT_KEEP_LEN + 64), which fits the
longest notice and leaves the output byte-identical for every list that fits.

Both readers walked the live array while sus_mount_keep_commit() was memset()ing
and memcpy()ing over it, so a read racing a commit could report a count that no
longer matched the entries it printed, or print an entry half old prefix and half
new one. Each read now copies the (length, entries) pair under mount_keep_lock and
prints from the copy: the lock covers the memcpy only, because seq_printf() grows
the seq buffer with kvmalloc(GFP_KERNEL) and must not run in an atomic section.
The copy is bounded by the same constant the array is, so the torn read is gone
without new state.
kernel: susfs (LKM): sus_path: expose the dirent verdict so it can be asked before emitting
kernel: susfs (LKM): sus_dirent: a getdents64 that never writes a hidden name to the caller
kernel: susfs (LKM): kstat: ask the pre-emission filter before falling back to the original getdents64

kernel: susfs (LKM): opath: two close-fd contracts, one prototype - the 6.1 change was missed

close_fd_get_file() kept its NAME across 6.1 and changed its prototype there:

  5.10..5.15  int close_fd_get_file(unsigned int fd, struct file **res)   fs/file.c:796
              takes the fd out and then get_file()s the file, so the caller owns TWO
              references and the kernel-doc asks for filp_close() and then an fput();
  6.1..6.6    struct file *close_fd_get_file(unsigned int fd)             fs/file.c:805
              same name, new prototype, no reference of its own;
  6.12..      struct file *file_close_fd(unsigned int fd)                 fs/file.c:784
              renamed, and "Doesn't take a separate reference count."

Both older shapes were resolved into one pointer carrying the 5.x prototype, so on 6.1/6.6 the
returned struct file * was read as an int status - non-zero, therefore "failed" - while the fd
was already out of the caller's table. The deny path then returned the caller its own dead
descriptor number: open appears to succeed and the next fstat is EBADF. The file it had just
been handed was never released either. The r18.2 fix (6785a68) covered only the 6.12 rename,
so 6.1 and 6.6 stayed broken.

The prototype is now chosen at build time from the kernel the variant is compiled for - the one
place the difference is visible - and the name is still resolved into it at run time, so a
vendor backport of either helper keeps working. The reference count stays a run-time fact: the
pre-6.1 helper took a reference of its own, its contract is therefore filp_close() AND an
fput() (two releases), and the deny path did one. Measured on 5.15: 5000 denies left nr_files
and filp slab objects up by ~5000, and they stayed up after the callers had exited and after
the module was unloaded.

kernel: susfs (LKM): or_entry: keep the descriptor's O_CLOEXEC, and narrow the flags like the kernel does

Two places where the name layer resolved things differently from the kernel it stands in for:

- O_CLOEXEC was stripped from the flags (it is not a property of the file) and then also used
  to allocate the descriptor, so a redirected openat2(..., O_CLOEXEC) came back without
  FD_CLOEXEC: it survives execve, and one fcntl(F_GETFD) reads the difference. The kernel takes
  that bit from the UNSTRIPPED how.flags (do_sys_openat2(): get_unused_fd_flags(how.flags &
  O_CLOEXEC)), so the descriptor flag is now kept separately, out of the narrowing.

- The lookup flags were computed from the flags as they arrived, while the kernel narrows them
  to O_PATH_FLAGS first whenever O_PATH is present - "O_PATH beats everything else." in
  build_open_how() (fs/open.c) - which drops O_CREAT/O_EXCL before LOOKUP_FOLLOW is decided.
  The layer stopped at the symlink and matched the rule table against the link, found nothing
  and passed the call back, while the kernel followed that link and opened its target: so
  `ln -s <rule target> <own path>` plus O_PATH|O_CREAT|O_EXCL stepped around the redirect.
  Measured on device with no module loaded: that call opens the link's target (an O_PATH fd,
  fstat reports a regular file), it is not -ELOOP. openat2 answers the same combination with
  EINVAL because it never calls build_open_how(), so its branch is left alone.

kernel: susfs (LKM): opath: declare the out-parameter only where it exists

The 6.1+ arm of opath_take_fd() calls the helper that returns the file itself, so the
out-parameter the older prototype needs does not exist there at all - and a variable for it is
-Wunused-variable, which this build runs as -Werror.  The 6.1/6.6/6.12/6.18 variants failed to
compile on it; 5.10/5.15 are the other arm and were fine.

kernel: susfs (LKM): or: scheme 4 asks KernelSU only about the uids KernelSU would umount for

UID_UMOUNTED_PROC stands in for upstream's TIF_PROC_UMOUNTED, and this module
answers it by asking KernelSU instead of reading the flag.  The two do not
agree for a uid KernelSU never asks about: ksu_uid_should_umount() returns
default_non_root_profile.umount_modules when it finds no profile, and that
value is TRUE (kernel/policy/allowlist.c:55), so uid 0, 1000 and 2000 all
answer "yes".  A scheme-4 rule was therefore applied to root, init,
system_server, the adb shell and su itself - none of which upstream's flag
ever covers, because the flag is only set on the umount path.

KernelSU reaches that path only for an app uid, the webview zygote or an
isolated process (kernel/feature/kernel_umount.c:93, with is_appuid() /
is_isolated_process() and the range constants from
kernel/policy/allowlist.h:8-13).  Keep that boundary before asking, so the
answer mirrors the flag rather than the question.

The app-uid half is deliberately not reused from
susfs_is_current_proc_umounted_app(): what earns scheme 4 its own predicate
is that it also covers the init-derived webview zygote (uid 1053), which sits
below 10000 and is inside the set above.

kernel: susfs (LKM): or_entry, opath: review follow-ups - fsnotify twice on 6.6+, O_TMPFILE vs the narrowing

An adversarial review of this branch turned up six things, all of them fixed here.

- 6.6 moved fsnotify_open() into do_dentry_open() (fs/open.c:985 there) and 6.12 split it out
  again into vfs_open() (:1095); filp_open() goes through both, so from 6.6 on the kernel has
  already reported a redirected open and our explicit call produced TWO IN_OPEN events for one
  open.  On 5.10..6.1 the only call sits in do_sys_openat2(), which a filp_open() never reaches -
  that is the one that has to stay.  The call is now inside
  `#if LINUX_VERSION_CODE < KERNEL_VERSION(6, 6, 0)`.

- The __O_TMPFILE pass-through sat BEFORE the O_PATH narrowing.  build_open_how() discards
  __O_TMPFILE whenever O_PATH is present, so `openat(p, O_PATH|__O_TMPFILE)` is a plain O_PATH
  open to the kernel: handing that combination back was one more open the kernel resolved while
  this layer never looked at it.  The check now sits after the narrowing; openat2 answers the
  same combination with EINVAL and is unaffected.

- opath: the note claimed that resolving by name still covers a vendor backport of either
  helper.  It cannot - the two shapes share a NAME, and a by-name resolver cannot see which
  prototype a kernel kept.  The note now states what the build-time choice covers, what it does
  not, and what each wrong direction would do (a second fput() on a reference it owns, or an
  out-parameter written through a register that was never set).

- Two comments quoted the upstream allocation call wrongly (do_sys_openat2() passes how->flags;
  alloc_fd() is what reads O_CLOEXEC out of it).

- build-ddk.yml still described close_fd_get_file() as returning a status on every kernel -
  exactly the model this branch replaces.

- tools/susfs_open_probe.c wrote the path argument into out[2048] with no bound, and a path can
  be far longer than that (MAX_ARG_STRLEN is 128 KiB).  It is truncated now.

kernel: susfs (LKM): sus_map: take the reference map_files_get_link() left with the caller

map_files_get_link() ends its success path with

	*path = vma->vm_file->f_path;
	path_get(path);

and its only caller releases that reference on the SUCCESS path alone
(proc_pid_readlink(): `if (error) goto out;` comes before `path_put(&path);`).  The map_files
probe turned the return value into -ENOENT so that a hidden mapping's symlink behaves like one
that is not there - and left that reference with nobody.  Every resolution of such a symlink
leaked a dentry and a mount reference; the mapped file keeps a reference of its own, so the
dentry is never reclaimed and the mount can never be unmounted, and an app uid reaches it in a
loop through the ranges /proc/self/map_files lists.

The reference now changes hands together with the answer.  It is released from task_work rather
than from the probe: the return handler runs in the exception context that fired the kprobe
(arm64 raises BRK for it), where sleeping is not allowed, and path_put() can sleep - dropping the
last reference reaches ->d_iput().  The work item is GFP_ATOMIC for the same reason.  If even
queueing it fails, the call keeps the kernel's own answer instead of leaking silently, and
map_stat reports it as putfail=.

Found by an audit of main@52f3d9d that read the callee's reference contract against the caller's
release path.

kernel: susfs (LKM): opath: take the file the check inspected, or give the fd back

Original change by supervooc (PR #87); rebased onto the release fix from #89 and with the
reference accounting corrected - see the last paragraph.

The post-check inspects a file via fget_raw(fd), decides, and only then takes the descriptor out
of the table - by NUMBER.  files_struct is shared (CLONE_FILES), so another thread of the same
task can close that number and open something else over it in between: the layer then removed and
fput()ed a file it had never inspected, while answering -ENOENT for an open that matched nothing.

The reference fget_raw() took is now held across the take, and the result is compared against it:

  victim != f   fd_install() puts that file back exactly where it was and the open stands (the
                counter says so); closing it would take away a descriptor this layer was never
                asked about, and -ENOENT would deny an open that matched nothing.
  victim == f   the descriptor goes away exactly as before.

The accounting on that second path is the part #87 got wrong.  How many references this path owns
depends on the helper the kernel has: fget_raw()'s and the take's are always there, and before 6.1
close_fd_get_file() adds a third of its own (fs/file.c: get_file(), after the fd is out of the
table).  So a pre-6.1 kernel needs three fput()s here and 6.1+ needs two - releasing two on 5.10/
5.15 still leaks one struct file per deny (measured on #87's own build: 2000 denies left file-nr
+1920), while a third on 6.1+ would be a refcount underflow.  The rollback path needs the same
care for the reference the helper added.

To be verified on the device before this is merged: 1000 app-uid O_PATH opens of a hidden node
(2000 denies) must leave file-nr and the filp slab flat, where the pre-#89 build showed +2016, and
the O_PATH answer for a hidden node must still be ENOENT.

kernel: susfs (LKM): sus_dirent: the name it is given is not a C string, and the two gates it skipped

Fixes the findings an adversarial review raised against the pre-emission filter, plus one more
from the same read.  (Original layer by Bouteillepleine, PR #85.)

- **filldir hands over (pointer, length), not a C string.**  The NUL the kernel relies on is one
  IT appends in the caller's buffer (filldir64 -> unsafe_copy_dirent_name), and a filesystem that
  passes on raw reply bytes never had one - fuse emits
  `dir_emit(ctx, dirent->name, dirent->namelen, ...)` straight out of its reply buffer, and that is
  how Android's /sdcard and /storage/emulated/* are served.  The predicate behind
  sus_path_dirent_hidden() uses strcmp(), so handing it that pointer read past namlen and, whenever
  the byte after the name was not a NUL, missed the match: the hidden name was written to the
  caller after all - the one thing this layer exists to prevent.  The name is copied into a
  terminated buffer first now, and a name that cannot be one (over NAME_MAX) is not matched.

- **The no_extra isolation switch was lost on this path.**  sus_path_dirent_filter() returns early
  when no_extra=1 - the layer is not registered at all then - but the pre-emission predicate did
  not, and a supercall can still register a rule afterwards: listings would then hide a file that
  stat/open still answer for, which is the mismatch the two-layer design exists to avoid.  The
  check now lives in sus_path_dirent_hidden(), so both entries into the predicate answer alike.

- **6.16 gave dir_context a `count` field**, which the kernel keeps as the remaining room and the
  filesystems read as their buffer-size hint (fuse: `clamp((unsigned int)ctx->count, PAGE_SIZE,
  max)`; overlayfs: passes it to the lower layer).  This layer left it 0, which reads as "no room":
  fuse clamps back to one page per call and overlayfs hands 0 downwards - measurably different from
  a stock 6.16+ kernel.  It is filled where the kernel has it and kept in step with the private
  counter.

- sd_name_ok() dropped half of verify_dirent_name(): the `len < PATH_MAX` bound.

kernel: susfs (LKM): or: scheme 4's uid boundary mirrors KernelSU's question, not SUSFS's flag

Original change by supervooc (PR #88).  The boundary itself is kept - an adversarial review
confirmed it matches the set KernelSU actually asks the umount question about - and the comments
that described it wrongly are corrected, because that description is what a future reader would
have believed.

Corrected:

- "the set its TIF_PROC_UMOUNTED flag can ever be set for".  That flag is SUSFS's, not KernelSU's
  (kernel_patches/include/linux/susfs_def.h:64); KernelSU's own tree does not contain it at all.
  It is set by kernel_patches/KernelSU/10_enable_susfs_for_ksu.patch, in kernel/hook/setuid_hook.c,
  for `is_isolated_process(ruid) || (is_appuid(ruid) && ksu_uid_should_umount(ruid))` - a narrower
  set than the one below: it never includes the webview zygote (uid 1053 fails both predicates) and
  it additionally requires the caller to be a zygote child.  kernel_umount.c:93 is the gate this
  set does mirror, and it is the one an unpatched KernelSU uses.

- "the webview zygote is one of them, and it is inside the set above".  It is inside the set this
  boundary mirrors - KernelSU asks about it - but the upstream flag is never SET for it.  The
  comment says that now, in those words.

- "everything KernelSU never umounts for - root, init, system_server, the adb shell, su itself - is
  answered false here".  That is true for the first four and not for su: the upstream flag is
  inherited across fork and never cleared (nothing calls susfs_clear_current_proc_umounted()), so a
  su descended from an already-umounted app still answers true upstream, while this boundary answers
  false for every uid outside the set.  The difference is deliberate - this gate mirrors the
  question the umount schemes are about, "would KernelSU umount for this uid", which has a definite
  answer for root/init/system_server/adb shell instead of the "no profile, therefore umount"
  default - and it is now written down instead of being denied.

kernel: susfs (LKM): open_redirect: hook every seq_show, not whichever one kallsyms lists first

fs/proc/fd.c's fdinfo callback is installed through `single_open(file, seq_show, inode)`, so it can
only be found by name - and above 5.15 that name is not unique: the DDK trees carry four symbols
called exactly `seq_show` on android14-6.1 and android15-6.6 (one on 5.10/5.15).  register_kprobe()
with .symbol_name attaches to the first one kallsyms happens to list, so on those kernels the fdinfo
rewrite can end up on an unrelated function and the reverse-disguise face silently stops working:
/proc/<pid>/fdinfo/N prints the real mnt_id/ino while mountinfo shows the disguised ones - a
one-file oracle, and the very failure sus_mount already hit and fixed by enumerating.

So: ksu_find_symbol_all("seq_show", ...) and hook every address (up to 8), and let the return
handler recognise fdinfo by the file it was given - m->file's dentry parent is named "fdinfo" - so
an unrelated seq_show costs one comparison and changes nothing.  Registration and teardown go
through the same array; the /proc readout still reports "an fdinfo probe is armed", and the log line
now says how many of how many symbols were hooked.

Found by an audit of main@52f3d9d (I-5).

manager: guard parseKernelVersion against non-Int version fields (https://github.com/tiann/KernelSU/pull/3593)

`parseKernelVersion` pulls three numeric groups out of the version
string and calls `.toInt()` on each:

```kotlin
KernelVersion(find.groupValues[1].toInt(), find.groupValues[2].toInt(), find.groupValues[3].toInt())
```

The input is `Os.uname().release`, which isn't guaranteed to be sane. If
any captured field is longer than `Int.MAX_VALUE` can hold, `toInt()`
throws `NumberFormatException` and takes the app down, even though the
function already has a `(-1, -1, -1)` sentinel for the "no match" case.

Switched to `toIntOrNull()` and fall back to that same sentinel when a
field can't be parsed, so a strange release string just reads as an
unknown version instead of crashing.

ksud: validate lengths when loading module config (https://github.com/tiann/KernelSU/pull/3598)

`save_config()` validates the entry count and every key/value against
the limits at the top of the file:

```rust
pub const MAX_CONFIG_KEY_LEN: usize = 256;
pub const MAX_CONFIG_VALUE_LEN: usize = 1024 * 1024;
pub const MAX_CONFIG_COUNT: usize = 32;
```

`load_config()` doesn't check any of them. It reads `count`, `key_len`
and `value_len` straight out of the file and uses them directly:

```rust
let key_len = u32::from_le_bytes(key_len_buf) as usize;
let mut key_buf = vec![0u8; key_len];
```

Since those are u32 fields, a damaged config file can ask us to allocate
up to 4GB. The `read_exact()` right after would fail, but the allocation
happens first, so ksud aborts instead of returning an error.

This applies the same three limits on the read path. Nothing changes for
files written by `save_config()`, since it can't produce values above
the limits in the first place.

ksud: don't panic on a broken zip in get_zip_uncompressed_size (https://github.com/tiann/KernelSU/pull/3591)

`get_zip_uncompressed_size` iterates the archive with
`by_index(i).unwrap()`. If any entry can't be read the `unwrap()` panics
and the whole ksud process dies.

This is reachable from `module install`: hand it a truncated or
corrupted zip and instead of a clean "failed to read module" error you
get a panic.

Since the function already returns `Result<u64>`, the simple fix is to
propagate the error with `?`:

```rust
let mut total: u64 = 0;
for i in 0..zip.len() {
    total += zip.by_index(i)?.size();
}
Ok(total)
```

No behavior change for valid archives.

ksud: Accept empty and long kallsyms tokens (https://github.com/tiann/KernelSU/pull/3804)

The kallsyms parser rejects empty tokens and limits each expanded token
to 256 bytes. Linux's generator can emit empty entries for unused token
slots, and expanded tokens can exceed 256 bytes. Both cases make valid
token tables invisible to kernel metadata recovery.

Accept empty entries and raise the length bound to 512, matching
`KSYM_NAME_LEN` in [Linux's kallsyms
generator](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v6.1/scripts/kallsyms.c).
Keep the token count, printable-byte checks, token-index validation, and
digit/letter checks.

Validation:

- Built the Linux v6.1 `scripts/kallsyms.c` generator and fed it symbol
maps producing 155 empty entries and a 300-byte expanded token. The
existing parser rejected both generated tables; the updated parser
recognizes both.
- Five regression tests exercise metadata recovery with empty tokens in
pre-6.4 and 6.4+ layouts, accept 257/512-byte tokens, and reject a
513-byte token, a non-ASCII token, and an incorrect token index.
- `cargo ndk -t arm64-v8a --platform 26 check --workspace`, Android

kernel: susfs (LKM): sus_path: answer readlink the way the stat family does, by changing the gate itself

do_readlinkat() reaches security_inode_readlink() and vfs_readlink() only when

        d_is_symlink(dentry) || inode->i_op->readlink

holds.  For a registered PLAIN FILE neither is true: the caller got -EINVAL - which says
"this path exists" - while the stat family answered ENOENT for the same path.  That
disagreement is itself the tell, and no LSM hook can close it, because on that path the
hook is not called at all (measured on device: the counter stayed at zero and the answer
stayed EINVAL).

So the gate is what changes.  A registered inode is pointed at a copy of its i_op whose
readlink slot is ours:

  - that makes the condition above true, so the face becomes reachable at all;
  - the slot then answers exactly what the stat family answers, because it asks the same
    question - sus_path_inode_hidden() - and therefore applies the same per-caller gate.
    One predicate, one answer; no path string is read, normalized or re-resolved, so
    there is no second lookup to race against;
  - it costs nothing on any other syscall path: no probe, no per-call work, and nothing
    written into read-only memory - the inode is a heap object, so an RKP/proca kernel
    does not care either.

The copy is shared per original i_op and lives as long as the module, so there is no
per-inode lifetime to manage: each entry restores inode->i_op before dropping its
ihold() (the iput() sites), and the copies are freed in sus_path_exit() once every entry
has been released.

Failing to allocate a copy does not fail the registration - the rule still hides
everything the other faces cover - and it is counted, so the readout says whether the
face is armed.

/proc/susfs_path now reports "readlink: enoent=<n> armfail=<n>".

Credit: @VictorGabriel7Dev found the readlinkat bypass; this is a different mechanism for
the same hole.

Add module preinit: run actions before SELinux policy loads (https://github.com/tiann/KernelSU/pull/3907)

Adds a **preinit** mechanism that lets a module run a few actions
**before the SELinux policy is loaded and before `init.rc` is parsed** —
e.g. load a kernel module, run a static program, or write to
procfs/sysfs. A module describes them in a `preinit/` directory:

```
mymodule/
└── preinit/
    ├── preinit.conf      # one action per line: insmod / exec / write
    └── ...               # .ko files, programs, ...
```

- **Kernel runner**: a static, nolibc-built runner is embedded in the
kernel module (`.incbin`) and staged in a shmem file at boot. When PID 1
execs `/system/bin/init selinux_setup`, the execve hook swaps the runner
in via `/proc/self/fd/N`. The runner parses each module's
`preinit.conf`, performs the actions, then execs the real init. A boot
counter disables preinit after 3 failed boots in a row.
- **ksud** syncs each enabled module's `preinit/` dir to the preinit
partition (manifest-based, incremental, within a space budget on the
small `/metadata`). Storage dir is `/metadata/vold/ksu` when available
(hidden, does not change `/metadata`'s link count), else
`/metadata/watchdog/ksu`, else `/metadata/ksu`. `ksud module preinit
status|reset` inspects per-module state and clears the boot counter.
- `boot-patch` / `boot-patch-v2` gain `--no-preinit` (sets the
`preinit=0` kernel parameter).
- **Manager** shows a warning tag on modules whose preinit content was
not applied (no space / error / bootloop).
- **Docs**: `preinit.conf` format, actions, space budget, bootloop
recovery (EN + zh_CN).

- Verified on a Redmi K80 (android14-6.1): runner runs before policy
load (process context `kernel`), `/metadata` write + fsync survives
reboot, bootloop counter parks and `reset` recovers, all conf actions
(insmod/exec/write, optional `?`, quoting, exit codes, output
forwarding). Confirmed with both v1 (ksuinit in init_boot) and v2 (ko
injected into boot). `--no-preinit` disables it (`preinit: disabled`).
Charger mode (`androidboot.mode=charger`) is skipped and does not bump
the counter. Data lands under `/metadata/vold/ksu` with the
`vold_metadata_file` label; `/metadata` root link count is unchanged.
- Builds pass for all 8 KMIs (android12-5.10 … android17-6.18).

manager: give ksu_ops a free_mark, and drain fsnotify marks before dropping the group

ksu_observer_exit() calls fsnotify_put_group() right after unwatch_one_dir(),
but a group's marks are released by a delayed work
(fsnotify_mark_destroy_workfn) which runs after synchronize_srcu() and calls
group->ops->free_mark(), reading mark->group on the way.

Two problems follow:

  - ksu_ops has no free_mark at all, and fsnotify_final_mark_destroy() calls it
    unconditionally (no NULL check).  The marks here come from kzalloc(), not
    from fsnotify_mark_cache, so ksu_free_mark() is what releases them;
  - the work is not drained: dropping the group first makes the callback read a
    freed group, and returning before the work has run at all lets the module be
    unloaded while the callback text is still pending.  Either way it is a
    use-after-free in fsnotify_mark_destroy_workfn.

Drain the marks first, then put the group, and give the ops a free_mark.

Reported in inforcqb/susfs4ksu-lkm#103 (panic in fsnotify_mark_destroy_workfn,
fault address 0xfffffffffffffffc, after the module was unloaded).

kernel: susfs (LKM): sus_map: probe show_map() too, for kernels that inline show_map_vma()

A vendor kernel (vivo 6.6.89, susfs4ksu-lkm#102) keeps an out-of-line
show_map_vma() in /proc/kallsyms, so the probe arms, but the call sites inside
show_map() are inlined and it never fires: map_stat reports hides=0 while the
mapping stays visible in /proc/<pid>/maps.

show_map() itself is what proc_pid_maps_op points at, reached through a
function pointer in data, so that call site cannot be inlined away.  Hook it as
well: both take (struct seq_file *, void *v) with the vma as the second
argument, so one handler serves them, and a hit at the outer layer returns
straight to the caller - the inner probe (where it is out of line) never sees
the same vma twice.

map_stat now reports armed=x/7, so the new arm result is visible there.

Handle execveat selinux_setup exec on Android 17 QPR3 (https://github.com/tiann/KernelSU/pull/3911)

On Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 (`DP11.260918.005`, Pixel 11 Pro Fold),
preinit never engages. The runner is staged at boot, but when second
stage starts KernelSU logs:

```
KernelSU: preinit: runner staged (66336 bytes)
KernelSU: preinit: selinux_setup not seen, dropping runner
```

First-stage init execs `/system/bin/init selinux_setup`, and later
`second_stage`, with `execveat` (syscall 281 on arm64) rather than
`execve`. Temporary logging added to `ksu_hook_execve_common()`
confirmed that both execs reach the handler:

```
pid1 exec nr=281 execveat=1 path='/system/bin/init' argv1='selinux_setup'
pid1 exec nr=281 execveat=1 path='/system/bin/init' argv1='second_stage'
```

The `second_stage` hook already handles `execveat` through
`ksu_execveat_hook_ksud()`. Only the preinit check is limited to
`execve` (`!execveat`), so it never sees the `selinux_setup` exec.

Also accept `execveat` from PID 1, unless it's an `AT_EMPTY_PATH` exec
of an fd, which has no path to swap. `ksu_preinit_handle_execve()` still
requires the absolute path `/system/bin/init` and `argv[1] ==
"selinux_setup"`, so the dirfd doesn't matter. The runner is executed
through the same `execveat` call, with its `/proc/self/fd/N` path
swapped in.

Nothing changes for devices whose init uses `execve`: the condition on
that path is unchanged. Other `execveat` calls from PID 1, such as
`second_stage`, are rejected by the existing path and `argv` checks and
continue through the normal handler, as before. Preinit stays one-shot:
once the runner has been claimed or released, the handler returns before
reading anything from userspace. `AT_EMPTY_PATH` execs are still
skipped.

Booted on Pixel 11 Pro Fold, QPR3 Beta 1:

- **Without the fix:** `preinit: selinux_setup not seen, dropping
runner`.
- **With the fix:** `preinit: exec runner via /proc/self/fd/8` at 1.76
s. The runner hands off to init about 50 ms later (`init: Opening
SELinux policy`), and the boot completes normally: second stage starts,
SELinux is enforcing, and `/proc/1/cmdline` is `/system/bin/init
second_stage`.

kernel: susfs (LKM): susfs: control nodes follow the su gate, and carry KernelSU's file label

Two changes that came out of the su-mechanism review, both about the module's own /proc nodes:

1. The gate was a hardcoded current_uid() == 0, which is neither the su rule nor what the module's own visibility predicate answers.  Every control node's open/write now asks susfs_control_visible(), which is __ksu_is_allow_uid_for_current() - the function sucompat calls through the ksu_is_allow_uid_for_current() macro - so forbid_system_uid, the always-allowed manager, the allowed-shell rule and the allowlist profile all apply.  sus_path's self-protect rules use the same gate, so the node names are visible to exactly the processes that could su.

2. The nodes were born under u:object_r:proc:s0, whose policy refuses even an adb shell the gate accepted.  They are now moved to u:object_r:ksu_file:s0 at load.  security_inode_setsecurity() has no registered hook on the Android 5.15 kernel (it answers -EOPNOTSUPP), so the SELinux field itself is written: inode_security_struct.sid at inode->i_security, walking selinux_blob_sizes.lbs_inode because that kernel already has per-LSM blobs.  Both offsets come from BTF with the member type checked, the write happens only when the field currently holds the proc label, and >= 6.4 is skipped.

Tested on PJA110 / Android 16 / 5.15.180: shell (may su) reads and writes the nodes, an unlisted app gets ENOENT, root works; 8 load/pressure/unload cycles and an rmmod-under-access race produce no crash reports.
kernel: susfs (LKM): susfs: put the relabel block before the layer table (it landed inside the struct)
kernel: susfs (LKM): susfs: declare susfs_btf_member_offset in the header too

kernel: susfs (LKM): control nodes: widen the su gate only where the ksu_file label is actually there

Since https://github.com/inforcqb/susfs4ksu-lkm/pull/106 the control nodes' gate is KernelSU's allow predicate, so adb shell,
Shizuku-style tools on the shell uid and su-granted apps pass it.  But the relabel
to u:object_r:ksu_file:s0 - what lets those callers actually read the nodes - is
skipped on >= 6.4, and can also fail or be partial elsewhere.  The nodes then keep
u:object_r:proc:s0, whose policy answers EACCES to exactly the callers the gate
just admitted.

That regresses the answer from ENOENT to EACCES: ENOENT says "nothing here",
EACCES says "it is here, you just cannot read it", so any shell-level caller can
prove the module is loaded with one `cat`.  Reported in susfs4ksu-lkm#108.

A gate can only be as wide as the set SELinux will also admit, so tie the two
together: susfs_control_relabelled is set by the relabel path only when every
control node it found now carries the ksu_file label, and the gate falls back to
root-only until then - which is what those nodes' labels say anyway.  The
all-or-nothing test keeps a partial relabel from widening the gate for the nodes
that did not get it.

On >= 6.4 the relabel returns early, so the flag stays false and the gate stays
root-only: back to the ENOENT the nodes had before https://github.com/inforcqb/susfs4ksu-lkm/pull/106, with no EACCES telling
anyone they exist.

Known residual, from the same report: below 6.4 the relabel is a one-time write at
load.  An inode that is evicted and recreated under proc's label later would
answer EACCES again while the flag still says the set is usable.  Reaching that
needs memory pressure plus a node's inode being dropped, and the proper fix is to
re-check the label per access instead of at load; left for a follow-up.

fix(kernel): align SELinux hide policy parsing (https://github.com/tiann/KernelSU/pull/3936)

Parsing the backup policy to completion before checking the live policy
leaves a one-parse failure path and a two-parse success path. A crafted
context can amplify that difference into a timing signal.

Check corresponding fields in both policies in the same pass, while
keeping policy-local IDs and validity checks separate. Reuse one mutable
context buffer and restore the MLS suffix before validating the live
context.

If live SID synchronization returns -ESTALE after a policy reload, drop
the RCU read lock, restore the input, and retry against the current
policy. Do not sync the live SID when backup conversion fails.

and tools/verify-gki.sh, and add the index map next to the module parameter so

A feature was advertised and its commands hijacked whether or not the layer
that implements it initialized: CONFIG_KSU_SUSFS_SUS_KSTAT stayed in

advertise-a-failed-capability shape a detector probes for.

  layer's init returns 0; create_gate/opath/dirent share SUS_PATH's bit
- SHOW_ENABLED_FEATURES reports an entry only while its bit is set

kernel: susfs (LKM): ksu_allow_gate: the version alone does not decide whether the warning is actionable

Below 6.4 the relabel can still be switched off: expose_proc=0 returns early
from susfs_relabel_control_nodes(), susfs_control_relabelled stays false and
susfs_control_visible() answers uid == 0 without ever asking KernelSU.  The
warning was still printed there, which is the same "names a problem that is
not one" the previous commit removed for 6.4 and up.

module parameter before any layer init, so it is already final here.

kernel: susfs (LKM): sus_path: say what readdir actually does with the placeholder, and what a fault leaves

Two comments were wrong about the code they describe:

- "readdir() skips records whose d_ino is 0 (bionic does)": neither bionic's
  __readdir_locked() nor glibc's readdir64() looks at d_ino; both step by
  d_reclen.  The placeholder is handed to the caller like any other record -
  one entry with an empty name - and the next readdir() continues after it.
  That is still better than ending the directory early, and it does not rely
  on a skip no libc performs.

- "A scrub stopped by a fault can only have zeroed bytes from name[0] onward -
  inside the first record, never its header": the clear runs from name_off to
  count, so a fault partway through leaves later records without headers too.
  The first record's own header does survive (the placeholder is written only
  after a successful scrub), and the fallback returns count, which then claims
  "nothing was filtered" over a chain that is no longer whole.  That is a
  copy_from_user fault inside the buffer the kernel itself produced, so it
  fails towards nothing of ours leaking; the comments now say so instead of
  claiming a parseable chain.

inode->i_op pointing at the module copy with orig_iop NULL, so
sus_path_iop_restore() became a no-op on retire and sus_path_iops_free() left a
dangling inode->i_op once the module unloaded - a UAF for any inode that
outlived it.

for the same path (sus_path_publish_entry()'s merge branch).

kernel: susfs (LKM): susfs_main: pass the fatal decision to the layer loader

Replace the per-layer fatal field with susfs_load_layer(id, fatal): the layer
table keeps name/init/exit/armed/feature, susfs_load_plan[] carries the load
order and the bool, and the loader owns the rollback-or-warn policy.  The plan
length is a build-time check and its id==position is checked before any layer
runs; any error rolls back every armed layer.  Behavior is unchanged: fp_hook,
lsm_hook, sus_path and supercall are fatal; the other fourteen keep their
previous non-fatal handling, including arming their feature when their init
succeeds.

kernel: susfs (LKM): sus_path: answer readlink ENOENT for confined callers

Add an inode_readlink LSM hook that returns -ENOENT for a registered dentry
before vfs_readlink(); otherwise the normal LSM decision is left in place (on
6.12+ the displaced SELinux function is run explicitly).  Report both readlink
counters in hide_list and add the hook to the CI prototype list.

Verified: 8-variant build and CFI gate on this branch; the author measured
android14-6.1 readlinkat before/after; no 6.12/6.18 device run.

kernel: susfs (LKM): sus_map: expose rules through /proc/susfs_map

Add add/del/clear writes and a read-only listing for the existing sus_map
rules, so scripts can manage them without a reboot(2) supercall.  Deleted
slots are reused and map_stat now reports active rules.

kernel: susfs (LKM): kernel: replace kprobes on indirect-call entries for BTI kernels

On a kernel built with CONFIG_ARM64_BTI_KERNEL, register_kprobe() overwrites
the entry instruction (bti c) with brk. Callers that reach the function through
a pointer - invoke_syscall() via sys_call_table, seq_read() via
seq_operations.show - then fault with "Oops - BTI" on the first call.

Swap the three affected entries for pointer replacements:
- supercall: sys_call_table[__NR_reboot] wrapper via susfs_fp_install()
- hide_syms: kallsyms_op/modules_op .show wrappers
- sus_map: proc_pid_maps_op/proc_pid_smaps_op .show wrappers

The seq_operations.show wrappers publish the saved original before the pointer
that reaches it (smp_wmb), decide before running the original (no count
rollback / timing gap), and drain in-flight callers on unload. The wrappers are
marked __nocfi: each one calls the saved kernel function through a pointer, so
the call site must not be CFI-instrumented.

Also make susfs_self_hide_nodes a global symbol: it was static, so the compiler
omitted a BTI landing pad; a long-call veneer then faulted during module init.

show_map_vma is a direct call and keeps its kprobe.

Tested on 6.18.21 (PYB110, same GKI release as #141): version handshake
v2.3.0, rule matrix 24 PASS / 0 FAIL, maps/smaps and kallsyms lines hidden,
plain reboot(2) forwards and returns EINVAL, load/rmmod clean. A same-kernel
reproduction with the unpatched build and BakaSU late-load faults with
"Oops - BTI"; a dispatcher-disabled control with this build runs clean.

kernel: susfs (LKM): supercall: fall back to kprobe when the sys_call_table cannot be hooked

792ac97 moved the reboot supercall from a kprobe to a sys_call_table hook
for BTI kernels. On arm64 GKI under pKVM the table page is EL2-protected, so
susfs_fp_install() finds no landing pad and the install fails; supercall being
a fatal layer, the module then refuses to load, taking the LSM sus_path hiding
down with it on a device where it works fine.

The two mechanisms cover disjoint kernels: a kprobe on the indirect-call entry
breaks on BTI, the table hook breaks under pKVM. So try the table first (keeps
BTI kernels working) and fall back to register_kprobe(__arm64_sys_reboot) when
it cannot arm. sus_map and sus_mount already use that kprobe path. A kernel that
is both BTI and pKVM takes neither and the layer still fails, as before.

kernel: Remove noisy logs from critical and frequent paths (https://github.com/tiann/KernelSU/pull/3960)

Updating root permissions currently logs every running thread while
local interrupts are disabled and `tasklist_lock` is held. On devices
with synchronous consoles, especially slow serial ports, `printk()` can
extend this atomic section long enough to delay IPIs and trigger a
watchdog reset.

[https://github.com/tiann/KernelSU/issues/3950](https://github.com/tiann/KernelSU/issues/3950) reports freezes
and reboots when granting or revoking root. The reporter [captured 65
mark and 2,050 unmark
messages](https://github.com/tiann/KernelSU/issues/3950#issuecomment-6525426190),
and [reported that removing the per-thread logs stopped the
freeze](https://github.com/tiann/KernelSU/issues/3950#issuecomment-6518813000).
Routine `handle_setresuid` and `hook_manager` exec messages also flood
the log during normal app and service startup without providing useful
diagnostics.

Remove routine process-marking output, allowlist dumps and per-entry
save/prune messages, input-probe logging, and debug output from the
ARM64/x86 `stop_machine` patching paths. Also remove repetitive
setresuid, Manager FD-install and init exec-tracking messages, and
rate-limit repeated ioctl diagnostics. Keep error reporting, moving
patch-failure diagnostics until after `stop_machine()` returns.

Test-only follow-up on revert/hide-syms-direct.

That's caused all usecase of selinux_inode become invalid and may cause
kernel panic

We use vmlinux.btf query for this struct to know the current offset of
lbs_inode to workaround this problem
This require CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF, but GKI enable that since
android13-5.15 [2]
So when it disabled, that's mean user is using Custom Kernel, and they
should compile intree.

Fix https://github.com/tiann/KernelSU/issues/3947

See more:

https://android.googlesource.com/kernel/common/+/41c5b269af8b1f0bffcab7766a793f294ae6764e

+ *   - syscall number is passed in r7
+ *   - arguments are in r0, r1, r2, r3, r4, r5

+

+#define _NOLIBC_SYSCALL_REG         "r7"
+#define _NOLIBC_THUMB_SET_R7        ""
+#define _NOLIBC_THUMB_RESTORE_R7    ""
+

+	register long _num  __asm__(_NOLIBC_SYSCALL_REG) = (num);             \
+	register long _arg1 __asm__ ("r0");                                   \
+									      \
+	__asm__ volatile (                                                    \
+		_NOLIBC_THUMB_SET_R7                                          \
+		"svc #0\n"                                                    \

+	register long _arg6 __asm__ ("r5") = (long)(arg6);                    \
+									      \

+		: "memory", "cc", "lr"                                        \
+	);                                                                    \
+	_arg1;                                                                \

+

+void __attribute__((weak, noreturn)) __nolibc_entrypoint __no_stack_protector _start(void)

+	__asm__ volatile (

+	);

+ *     preserved. See: https://www.linux-mips.org/wiki/Syscall as well as

+ *     the syscall's return value as a signed long value which is often either
+ *     a pointer or the negated errno value.

+ *   - The second level is mostly architecture-independent. It is made of

+ * to be done here as well.  Two things are: the arm64 O_LARGEFILE bit the syscall adds on the entries
+ * that set it (otherwise every redirected fd differs from every other fd in one bit that
+ * fcntl(F_GETFL) and the fdinfo `flags:` line both read), and the IN_OPEN notification where the
+ * kernel happens to have an out-of-line fsnotify_open() - it is a static inline on every tree, and
+ * the log says so where it is missing.  What is deliberately NOT reproduced, and is therefore handed
+ * back to the kernel instead:
+ *   - the flags openat2 would refuse (it validates its structure field by field, where the older
+ *     entries clean invalid values up and carry on), along with its `resolve`/`usize` (EINVAL/E2BIG,
+ *     and RESOLVE_* is applied during the walk) - finishing such an open would answer success where
+ *     the kernel answers an error, or answer with weaker semantics;
+ *   - O_TMPFILE, which is not a path open in the sense filp_open() models.
+ * Not covered at all, by construction: this is a syscall entry, so covers openat/openat2 and the
+ * three compat variants.  io_uring's OPENAT/OPENAT2, AArch32 `creat`, open_by_handle_at, execve and
+ * in-kernel filp_open() callers never come through here (upstream's do_sys_openat2 patch has the same
+ * boundary except for compat `creat`, which upstream also misses).
+ *
+ * On by default (module parameter or_entry).  It used to be opt-in, back when the vfs_open probe was
+ * still the default forward direction; that probe is gone, so this layer IS the forward direction -
+ * which is also why or_register() refuses a rule while it is not armed, and why an unarmed layer
+ * says so in the log instead of failing silently.
+ */
+#include <linux/kernel.h>
+#include <linux/version.h>	/* LINUX_VERSION_CODE: fsnotify_open() moved into the open path at 6.6 */
+#include <linux/module.h>
+#include <linux/fs.h>
+#include <linux/file.h>
+#include <linux/fcntl.h>	/* AT_FDCWD, O_CLOEXEC, __O_TMPFILE */
+#include <linux/path.h>		/* path_put() */
+#include <linux/namei.h>	/* getname_flags/filename_lookup prototypes, LOOKUP_FOLLOW */
+#include <linux/dcache.h>
+#include <linux/mount.h>
+#include <linux/uaccess.h>
+#include <linux/err.h>
+#include <linux/atomic.h>
+#include <linux/limits.h>
+#include "susfs.h"
+#include "susfs_log.h"
+#include "symbol_resolver.h"
+#include "susfs_or_entry.h"

+/* include/uapi/linux/openat2.h: three u64 fields, identical on both ABIs we build for. */
+struct susfs_open_how {
+	__u64 flags;
+	__u64 mode;
+	__u64 resolve;
+};
+
+/* The flag set the kernel's own build_open_flags() accepts (fs/open.c VALID_OPEN_FLAGS, which is
+ * built from exactly these uapi bits).  A flag outside it makes the kernel return EINVAL, so such a
+ * call is handed back rather than answered: filp_open() masks unknown bits away and would turn that
+ * EINVAL into a successful open.  This is deliberately the conservative direction - a bit that is
+ * legal on some kernel but missing here only means that open is not redirected. */
+#define SUSFS_OR_KNOWN_FLAGS							\
+	(O_RDONLY | O_WRONLY | O_RDWR | O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_NOCTTY | O_TRUNC |	\
+	 O_APPEND | O_NONBLOCK | O_NDELAY | __O_SYNC | O_DSYNC | FASYNC |	\
+	 O_DIRECT | O_LARGEFILE | O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NOATIME |		\
+	 O_CLOEXEC | O_PATH | __O_TMPFILE)
+
+/* fs/open.c's own O_PATH_FLAGS, and what build_open_how() narrows the flags to whenever O_PATH is
+ * present ("O_PATH beats everything else.").  Only these four bits survive that narrowing, so
+ * everything a caller sends alongside O_PATH - O_CREAT, O_EXCL, O_TRUNC - is gone before the kernel
+ * works out the lookup flags of the call.  It lives as a #define inside fs/open.c rather than in a
+ * header, hence spelled out here; O_CLOEXEC being in the set is also why a descriptor's own flag
+ * survives the narrowing. */
+#define SUSFS_OR_PATH_FLAGS	(O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_PATH | O_CLOEXEC)
+
+/* openat2's resolve bits (uapi/linux/openat2.h) and the lookup flags the kernel turns them into. */
+#define SUSFS_RESOLVE_NO_XDEV		0x01
+#define SUSFS_RESOLVE_NO_MAGICLINKS	0x02
+#define SUSFS_RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS	0x04
+#define SUSFS_RESOLVE_BENEATH		0x08
+#define SUSFS_RESOLVE_IN_ROOT		0x10
+#define SUSFS_RESOLVE_CACHED		0x20
+#define SUSFS_OR_KNOWN_RESOLVE							\
+	(SUSFS_RESOLVE_NO_XDEV | SUSFS_RESOLVE_NO_MAGICLINKS |			\
+	 SUSFS_RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS | SUSFS_RESOLVE_BENEATH |			\
+	 SUSFS_RESOLVE_IN_ROOT | SUSFS_RESOLVE_CACHED)
+
+/* The lookup flags for the source path, translated the way the kernel translates them for the open
+ * it would have done (fs/open.c, before do_filp_open): O_NOFOLLOW stops at the last component and
+ * O_CREAT|O_EXCL implies it, O_DIRECTORY demands a directory, and openat2's resolve bits map onto
+ * the matching LOOKUP_* bits.  A resolve bit this kernel has no lookup flag for (LOOKUP_CACHED
+ * arrived later than the others) is not mapped - the caller then gets a lookup with weaker
+ * semantics, which is why or_entry_redirect() rejects those calls instead of answering them. */
+static unsigned int or_lookup_flags(unsigned long flags, unsigned long resolve)
+{
+	unsigned int lflags = 0;
+
+	if (!(flags & O_NOFOLLOW) &&
+	    (flags & (O_CREAT | O_EXCL)) != (O_CREAT | O_EXCL))
+		lflags |= LOOKUP_FOLLOW;
+	if (flags & O_DIRECTORY)
+		lflags |= LOOKUP_DIRECTORY;
+	if (resolve & SUSFS_RESOLVE_NO_XDEV)
+		lflags |= LOOKUP_NO_XDEV;
+	if (resolve & SUSFS_RESOLVE_NO_MAGICLINKS)
+		lflags |= LOOKUP_NO_MAGICLINKS;
+	if (resolve & SUSFS_RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS)
+		lflags |= LOOKUP_NO_SYMLINKS;
+	if (resolve & SUSFS_RESOLVE_BENEATH)
+		lflags |= LOOKUP_BENEATH;
+	if (resolve & SUSFS_RESOLVE_IN_ROOT)
+		lflags |= LOOKUP_IN_ROOT;
+#ifdef LOOKUP_CACHED
+	if (resolve & SUSFS_RESOLVE_CACHED)
+		lflags |= LOOKUP_CACHED;
+#endif
+	return lflags;
+}

+/* Every one of these is resolved by name at load; see the header comment for which are exported. */
+static struct filename *(*or_getname_flags_fn)(const char __user *name, int flags, int *empty);
+static int (*or_filename_lookup_fn)(int dfd, struct filename *name, unsigned flags,
+				    struct path *path, struct path *root);
+static void (*or_putname_fn)(struct filename *name);
+static struct file *(*or_filp_open_fn)(const char *name, int flags, umode_t mode);
+static int (*or_get_unused_fd_flags_fn)(unsigned flags);
+static void (*or_fd_install_fn)(unsigned int fd, struct file *file);
+static void (*or_put_unused_fd_fn)(unsigned int fd);
+static void (*or_fsnotify_open_fn)(struct file *file);
+static int (*or_check_zeroed_user_fn)(const void __user *from, unsigned long count);
+
+static bool or_entry_ready;
+static atomic_t or_entry_hits = ATOMIC_INIT(0);
+
+/* On by default: this IS the forward direction now (the vfs_open probe is gone from
+ * susfs_open_redirect.c).  Off means the layer is not armed at all - see
+ * susfs_or_entry_init() - so a rule is refused rather than accepted and inert. */
+static bool or_entry_param = true;
+module_param_named(or_entry, or_entry_param, bool, 0600);
+
+susfs_or_entry_fn_t susfs_or_entry_hook;
+
+/* Indirect call into the kernel for the one notification the skipped syscall would have sent, so it
+ * sits in a __nocfi noinline function like every other one in this module (tools/cfi_sites.py fails
+ * the build on an instrumented call site).  A kernel without the symbol only loses the notification,
+ * which is why this one may be NULL. */
+static __nocfi noinline void or_fsnotify_open(struct file *file)
+{
+	if (or_fsnotify_open_fn)
+		or_fsnotify_open_fn(file);
+}
+
+/* Same shape for copy_struct_from_user()'s zero check: it is the helper openat2 uses to accept a
+ * structure larger than this kernel's, and it is a real exported symbol even though the macro that
+ * calls it is not. */
+static __nocfi noinline int or_check_zeroed_user(const void __user *from, unsigned long count)
+{
+	return or_check_zeroed_user_fn(from, count);
+}
+
+/* The undo of get_unused_fd_flags(): needed to keep the kernel's own order (descriptor first, file
+ * second), where a failed open leaves nothing behind. */
+static __nocfi noinline void or_put_unused_fd(unsigned int fd)
+{
+	or_put_unused_fd_fn(fd);
+}
+
+/* The original syscall is not called at all when this redirects, so nothing has to be undone if the
+ * process is killed mid-way; the fd is installed last, which is the same order the kernel uses.
+ *
+ * __nocfi noinline is mandatory for every call through a runtime-resolved pointer (the rule
+ * tools/cfi_sites.py enforces on the artifacts): without it, CFI instrumentation lands in whichever
+ * function this ends up in - the opath wrapper - and a checked indirect call into the kernel is a
+ * panic rather than an error return.  This is also why every kernel function above is held in a
+ * plain pointer and called from here, never from the wrapper itself. */
+static __nocfi noinline long or_entry_redirect(const struct pt_regs *regs, int kind)
+{
+	const char __user *uname = NULL;
+	unsigned long flags = 0, mode = 0, resolve = 0, usize = 0, o2flags = 0;
+	/* The descriptor's own flag, kept out of the narrowing the file flags go through: the kernel
+	 * takes it from the UNSTRIPPED flags when it allocates a descriptor (do_sys_openat2():
+	 * get_unused_fd_flags(how->flags), where alloc_fd() reads O_CLOEXEC), and losing it hands back a fd that survives
+	 * execve - a difference one fcntl(F_GETFD) reads. */
+	unsigned int fd_cloexec = 0;
+	struct susfs_open_how how;
+	struct filename *name;
+	struct path path;
+	char target[SUSFS_OR_PATH_MAX];	/* filled by susfs_open_redirect_match_path() under rcu */
+	struct file *f;
+	int dfd = AT_FDCWD;
+	long res;
+	int fd;
+
+	if (!or_entry_ready)
+		return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+
+	/* This hook is reached for every open() on the system, so the empty case has to be one load: no
+	 * live rules means nothing to resolve a name for, and deleting the last rule takes that cost away
+	 * again (susfs_open_redirect_rules counts live rules, not rules ever added). */
+	if (!susfs_open_redirect_active())
+		return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+
+	/* arm64 keeps a syscall's arguments in regs[0..5] for native and compat alike, so the
+	 * argument number IS the register index (arch/arm64/include/asm/syscall_wrapper.h). */
+	switch (kind) {
+	case SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_OPENAT:
+	case SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_COMPAT_OPENAT:
+		dfd = (int)regs->regs[0];
+		uname = (const char __user *)regs->regs[1];
+		/* Truncated to what the kernel's own declaration is: these entries take an `int flags`
+		 * and the syscall wrapper casts the register to it (__SC_CAST), so the upper half of the
+		 * register is ignored by the kernel.  Keeping it here would make the unknown-bit test
+		 * below see a "flag the kernel would reject" and hand a call the kernel resolves as a
+		 * plain open straight back to it - i.e. the redirect would be bypassable with
+		 * `flags | (1UL << 32)`.  openat2 is the exception and stays 64-bit, because the kernel
+		 * does not mask how.flags. */
+		flags = (unsigned int)regs->regs[2];
+		mode = regs->regs[3];
+		break;
+	case SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_COMPAT_OPEN:
+		/* COMPAT_SYSCALL_DEFINE3: no dirfd, so the arguments shift down by one. */
+		uname = (const char __user *)regs->regs[0];
+		flags = (unsigned int)regs->regs[1];
+		mode = regs->regs[2];
+		break;
+	case SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_OPENAT2:
+	case SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_COMPAT_OPENAT2:
+		dfd = (int)regs->regs[0];
+		uname = (const char __user *)regs->regs[1];
+		usize = regs->regs[3];
+		/* The kernel's own rules for this structure: a size below it is EINVAL, a size above it
+		 * is accepted as long as the bytes this kernel does not know are zero (that is what
+		 * copy_struct_from_user() checks, through check_zeroed_user()), and anything else is
+		 * E2BIG.  A call that gets here and is then not redirected still opens the real file, so
+		 * "we cannot be bothered" is not an option for a size the kernel would have accepted:
+		 * those go through when the helper is resolvable, and only fall back to the kernel where
+		 * it is not. */
+		if (usize < sizeof(how))
+			return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+		if (copy_from_user(&how, (const void __user *)regs->regs[2], sizeof(how)))
+			return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+		if (usize > sizeof(how) &&
+		    (!or_check_zeroed_user_fn ||
+		     or_check_zeroed_user((const void __user *)regs->regs[2] + sizeof(how),
+					  usize - sizeof(how)) <= 0))
+			return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+		/* ... and the two bits the kernel removes from these flags before it looks at any of them
+		 * (FMODE_NONOTIFY, which the caller is not supposed to see, and O_CLOEXEC, which belongs
+		 * to the descriptor).  Everything below is judged on what is left, exactly like the
+		 * kernel does: FMODE_NONOTIFY is not one of O_PATH_FLAGS, so judging the raw flags would
+		 * turn a legal `O_PATH|FMODE_NONOTIFY` open into "a flag the kernel would refuse" and hand
+		 * the call back to a kernel that opens the real file. */
+		/* O_CLOEXEC is stripped from the copy everything below judges, because it is not a
+		 * property of the file - but it belongs to the DESCRIPTOR, and the kernel keeps it for
+		 * exactly the moment it allocates one: do_sys_openat2() calls
+		 * get_unused_fd_flags(how->flags), where alloc_fd() reads O_CLOEXEC.  Dropping it here
+		 * (this branch assigns flags = o2flags a few lines down, and that copy is what the
+		 * descriptor was allocated from) gave every redirected openat2(..., O_CLOEXEC) a fd
+		 * without FD_CLOEXEC: it survives execve, and fcntl(F_GETFD) says so in one call. */
+		fd_cloexec = (unsigned int)(how.flags & O_CLOEXEC);
+		o2flags = how.flags & ~(unsigned long)(FMODE_NONOTIFY | O_CLOEXEC);
+		/* A resolve bit the kernel does not know is EINVAL, and EINVAL is an answer we cannot
+		 * give: it comes from the kernel.  A bit it does know is mapped onto the same LOOKUP_*
+		 * flags it would use (see or_lookup_flags()), so the caller's resolve semantics still
+		 * hold for the path this layer looks up itself. */
+		if (how.resolve & ~SUSFS_OR_KNOWN_RESOLVE)
+			return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+		/* The two combinations the kernel refuses before it looks at anything: RESOLVE_BENEATH
+		 * together with RESOLVE_IN_ROOT is EINVAL, and RESOLVE_CACHED with a call that would
+		 * create or truncate is EAGAIN (it will not fall back to a normal lookup).  Both are
+		 * answered by the kernel rather than by us - the second one is not just a difference in
+		 * the answer, it is a rule target that would be created or truncated.  The mask is the
+		 * kernel's own spelling, which is EAGAIN for a plain O_DIRECTORY too. */
+		if ((how.resolve & SUSFS_RESOLVE_BENEATH) && (how.resolve & SUSFS_RESOLVE_IN_ROOT))
+			return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+		if ((how.resolve & SUSFS_RESOLVE_CACHED) &&
+		    (o2flags & (O_TRUNC | O_CREAT | O_TMPFILE)))
+			return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+#ifndef LOOKUP_CACHED
+		/* This kernel cannot honour RESOLVE_CACHED, and answering the call with a normal lookup
+		 * would succeed where the kernel answers EAGAIN (it refuses to touch the disk for it). */
+		if (how.resolve & SUSFS_RESOLVE_CACHED)
+			return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+#endif
+		resolve = how.resolve;
+		/* openat2 validates every field of the structure, where the older syscalls silently
+		 * clean invalid values up (build_open_flags(): mode & ~S_IALLUGO is EINVAL when the
+		 * call creates something, non-zero mode otherwise, and filp_open() would strip both
+		 * before the kernel could object).  Answering such a call with a successful open is the
+		 * one outcome we must not produce, so it goes back too. */
+		if ((o2flags & (O_CREAT | __O_TMPFILE)) ? (how.mode & ~S_IALLUGO) : how.mode)
+			return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+		/* openat2 does not pass through build_open_how(), so the kernel tests its O_PATH rule
+		 * against these same stripped flags: anything besides O_PATH_FLAGS is EINVAL there, while
+		 * filp_open() would quietly mask those bits away and open the file. */
+		if ((o2flags & O_PATH) &&
+		    (o2flags & ~(unsigned long)(O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_PATH | O_CLOEXEC)))
+			return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+		flags = o2flags;
+		mode = how.mode;
+		break;
+	default:
+		return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+	}
+
+	/* The flags are handled the way the kernel handles them per entry, because that
+	 * differs: openat2 validates every field and answers EINVAL for a flag it does not know
+	 * (fs/open.c: build_open_flags() tests the raw how.flags), while open/openat/compat clean the
+	 * invalid bits away first (build_open_how(): `flags & VALID_OPEN_FLAGS`) and then open the file
+	 * as if they had not been passed.  Treating an unknown bit as "the kernel will refuse this" on
+	 * the older entries would hand the call back to a kernel that happily opens the real file - a
+	 * one-bit bypass of the redirect, and a cheaper one than any of the above.  So the older entries
+	 * get the same mask the kernel applies, and only openat2 can be declined over a flag. */
+	if (kind == SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_OPENAT2 || kind == SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_COMPAT_OPENAT2) {
+		/* Those two bits were already removed in the branch above, before its first check - the
+		 * kernel removes them before any of its own.  What is left is the gate the kernel applies
+		 * to these flags (build_open_flags(): `flags & ~VALID_OPEN_FLAGS` is EINVAL). */
+		if (flags & ~SUSFS_OR_KNOWN_FLAGS)
+			return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+	} else {
+		flags &= SUSFS_OR_KNOWN_FLAGS;
+		/* The kernel narrows O_PATH before anything else looks at the flags - "O_PATH beats
+		 * everything else." in build_open_how() - so by the time build_open_flags() works out
+		 * whether the last component is followed, an O_CREAT/O_EXCL that arrived alongside
+		 * O_PATH is already gone.  Judging the flags as they arrived made this layer resolve a
+		 * DIFFERENT name than the kernel resolves: it saw O_CREAT|O_EXCL, withheld
+		 * LOOKUP_FOLLOW, and matched the rule table against the symlink itself, while the
+		 * kernel followed that symlink and opened its target.  So a caller who writes
+		 * `ln -s <rule target> <a path of his own>` and then asks for O_PATH|O_CREAT|O_EXCL
+		 * was handed the un-redirected file - the redirect stepped around without ever touching
+		 * the rule table.  Narrowed here, both layers walk the same name.
+		 *
+		 * (openat2 does not narrow: it never calls build_open_how(), and build_open_flags()
+		 * answers that same combination with EINVAL - which is why the branch above is left
+		 * alone.) */
+		if (flags & O_PATH)
+			flags &= SUSFS_OR_PATH_FLAGS;
+		/* From the same function: a call that cannot create carries no mode, and an O_PATH
+		 * open never can. */
+		if (flags & O_PATH)
+			mode = 0;
+		/* O_CLOEXEC survives the narrowing above (it is one of O_PATH_FLAGS), so the
+		 * descriptor's flag is read from the flags the kernel would allocate it from. */
+		fd_cloexec = (unsigned int)(flags & O_CLOEXEC);
+	}
+
+	/* O_TMPFILE is not a path open in the sense filp_open() models (it needs the O_DIRECTORY part
+	 * handled by the caller's dirfd), so those are left to the kernel untouched.  This check sits
+	 * AFTER the narrowing above on purpose: build_open_how() discards __O_TMPFILE whenever O_PATH is
+	 * present, so `openat(p, O_PATH|__O_TMPFILE)` is a plain O_PATH open to the kernel - handing
+	 * that combination back here would leave one more open the kernel resolves while this layer
+	 * never looked at it.  (openat2 answers the same combination with EINVAL instead, and the
+	 * branch above already passes such a call through.) */
+	if (flags & __O_TMPFILE)
+		return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+
+	/* Which inode is the caller opening?  The lookup flags are the kernel's own translation of the
+	 * caller's flags and of openat2's resolve bits (fs/open.c, right before do_filp_open): with
+	 * LOOKUP_FOLLOW hard-wired, a caller's O_NOFOLLOW turned its ELOOP into a successful redirect -
+	 * a difference from a kernel without this module, and one that also tells an observer which
+	 * paths carry a rule (write a symlink to the path and open it with O_NOFOLLOW).  A path that
+	 * does not resolve (O_CREAT of a new file) cannot be the target of a rule, so the kernel is
+	 * left to answer it. */
+	name = or_getname_flags_fn(uname, 0, NULL);
+	if (IS_ERR(name))
+		return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+	res = or_filename_lookup_fn(dfd, name, or_lookup_flags(flags, resolve), &path, NULL);
+#if LINUX_VERSION_CODE < KERNEL_VERSION(5, 15, 0)
+	/* filename_lookup() consumed `name` through 5.14; 5.15 made the caller own it.
+	 * Putting it here again double-frees and panics (the create_gate 5.10 KE). */
+#else
+	or_putname_fn(name);
+#endif
+	if (res)
+		return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+
+	/* The target name is copied out of the rule while the lookup holds rcu_read_lock (rule slots are
+	 * recycled after a grace period, so nothing inside an entry may be used after this call). */
+	if (!susfs_open_redirect_match_path(&path, target, sizeof(target))) {
+		path_put(&path);
+		return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+	}
+	path_put(&path);	/* no reference is kept anywhere: the rule owns none either */
+	/* Defensive: an empty name is not a path, and filp_open("") resolves to the caller's own
+	 * working directory, i.e. it would hand out an unrelated fd. */
+	if (!target[0])
+		return SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS;
+
+	/* arm64 always opens with O_LARGEFILE (force_o_largefile() is `!IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_ARCH_32BIT_OFF_T)`,
+	 * and the syscall adds it before anything else looks at the flags).  Without it the fd we hand
+	 * back differs from every other fd in one visible bit: fcntl(F_GETFL) and the `flags:` line of
+	 * /proc/self/fdinfo/N both read f_flags directly.  CLOEXEC is the fd table's business, not the
+	 * open's - the kernel strips it before build_open_flags() sees it - so it is masked off here.
+	 *
+	 * The compat entries are the exception: the kernel deliberately does not set the bit there
+	 * ("Exactly like sys_openat(), except that it doesn't set the O_LARGEFILE flag"), and compat
+	 * openat2 does, because it is the same implementation as the native one.  An O_PATH open does
+	 * not carry it either - build_open_how() masks O_PATH opens to O_PATH_FLAGS. */
+#ifdef __aarch64__
+	if (!(flags & O_PATH) &&
+	    kind != SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_COMPAT_OPEN && kind != SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_COMPAT_OPENAT)
+		flags |= O_LARGEFILE;
+#endif
+	/* The descriptor is taken BEFORE the file is opened, which is the order do_sys_openat2() uses:
+	 * an EMFILE/ENFILE open then touches nothing at all, where opening first would have created or
+	 * truncated the rule's target and then failed anyway. */
+	fd = or_get_unused_fd_flags_fn(fd_cloexec);
+	if (fd < 0)
+		return fd;
+
+	f = or_filp_open_fn(target, (int)(flags & ~O_CLOEXEC), (umode_t)mode);
+	if (IS_ERR(f)) {
+		or_put_unused_fd((unsigned)fd);
+		return PTR_ERR(f);
+	}
+

+#ifndef __SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_H
+#define __SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_H
+
+#include <linux/limits.h>
+#include <linux/ptrace.h>
+
+/* The syscall entries susfs_opath.c replaces.  open_redirect's name-layer redirection is asked
+ * inside that wrapper rather than installing a wrapper of its own: one syscall entry can have
+ * exactly one, and those five belong to the O_PATH layer (which already needs every argument the
+ * name layer needs, so nothing is duplicated by sharing).
+ *
+ * The layer is optional at run time: susfs_or_entry_hook stays NULL until the open_redirect layer
+ * found every symbol it needs, and the wrapper tests it before each call, so a missing symbol
+ * costs nothing but the feature. */
+enum susfs_or_entry_kind {
+	SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_OPENAT = 0,
+	SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_OPENAT2,
+	SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_COMPAT_OPEN,
+	SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_COMPAT_OPENAT,
+	SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_COMPAT_OPENAT2,
+	SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_KIND_COUNT,
+};
+
+/* Returned when the hook did not redirect: the caller then runs the original syscall.  LONG_MIN
+ * cannot be a real answer here (a fd or -errno), so a mistake cannot be mistaken for one. */
+#define SUSFS_OR_ENTRY_PASS	LONG_MIN

+typedef long (*susfs_or_entry_fn_t)(const struct pt_regs *regs, int kind);
+
+extern susfs_or_entry_fn_t susfs_or_entry_hook;

+/* True once redirection can actually happen.  The open_redirect layer checks this when a rule is added:
+ * a rule that cannot fire is worse than no rule, so it refuses rather than register one. */
+static inline bool susfs_or_entry_armed(void)
+{
+	return READ_ONCE(susfs_or_entry_hook) != NULL;

+int susfs_or_entry_init(void);
+void susfs_or_entry_exit(void);
